alt: Arid landform sequence from a mountain front: steep bare rock, a sharp break of slope, a gently sloping pediment that falls 14 m in 700 m (2 percent, 1.1 degrees), alluvial fans that merge into a bajada, and a flat playa of salt and silt in the basin of internal drainage.
caption: Figure: mountain front, pediment, alluvial fans, bajada and playa (schematic, height exaggerated)

alt: Beach profiles compared: the shingle beach rises 2.7 m in 18 m (a gradient of 0.15, 15 percent, 8.5 degrees) while the sandy beach rises only 1.4 m in 70 m (0.02, 2 percent, 1.1 degrees), because swash sinks into permeable shingle and the weak backwash cannot pull it down.
caption: Figure: shingle and sandy beach profiles drawn from the worked-example measurements (height scale exaggerated)

alt: Sequence of headland landforms: waves widen a joint into a cave, a cave cut right through the headland makes an arch, the roof collapses to leave a stack, and further erosion and weathering reduce the stack to a stump.
caption: Figure: cave, arch, stack and stump (schematic sequence)

alt: Two channels drawn to the same scale: the upper-course channel (3 m wide, 0.5 m deep) has a hydraulic radius of 0.375 m, while the lower-course channel (20 m wide, 3 m deep) has 2.31 m, about six times more efficient because less of the water touches the bed and banks; the wetted perimeter is the thick line.
caption: Figure: wetted perimeter and hydraulic radius of an upper and a lower channel (worked-example values)

alt: Cliff and shore platform: waves cut a notch at the foot of a 15 m cliff, the cliff collapses and retreats 36 m in 18 years (2 m a year), and a very gentle platform 160 m wide that falls only 2.8 m (1 in 57, about 1 degree) is left behind; the height scale is exaggerated.
caption: Figure: cliff retreat, wave-cut notch and shore platform (values from the lesson examples, height exaggerated about four times)

alt: Passage of a cold front at a station: pressure falls to a minimum of 1004 hPa at 12:00 then rises 10 hPa to 1014 hPa by 18:00, while temperature falls 12 degrees C from 27 at 12:00 to 15 at 18:00, most of it between 12:00 and 15:00 when the front passes.
caption: Figure: pressure and temperature readings during the passage of a cold front (data from the worked example)

alt: Concordant and discordant coasts in plan: on a concordant coast the rock bands run parallel to the coast and give a fairly straight shoreline, while on a discordant coast bands of hard and soft rock meet the sea at right angles, so resistant rock forms headlands and soft rock forms bays.
caption: Figure: concordant and discordant coastlines compared (plan view, schematic)

alt: Demographic transition model: birth and death rates are both high in stage 1; the death rate falls first in stage 2, so the gap (natural increase) widens; in stage 3 the birth rate falls and the gap narrows; in stage 4 both are low; in stage 5 the birth rate may fall below the death rate.
caption: Figure: birth and death rates through the five stages of the demographic transition model (schematic)

alt: Temperature through a day: on the clear day it falls to 8 degrees C at 06:00 and peaks at 28 degrees C at 15:00, a range of 20 degrees; on the cloudy day it stays between 14 and 22 degrees, a range of 8 degrees, because cloud cuts daytime heating and traps heat at night.
caption: Figure: temperature every three hours on a clear day and a cloudy day (illustrative highveld data)

alt: Drainage basin as an open system: precipitation of 840 mm is the input; evapotranspiration of 640 mm and runoff of 150 mm leave, so storage rises by 50 mm (P = Q + E + change in storage). Stores and flows (interception, infiltration, overland flow, throughflow, percolation, groundwater flow) are labelled.
caption: Figure: stores, transfers and the water balance of the worked-example catchment (illustrative data)

alt: Three dune types in plan: a barchan is a crescent with its horns pointing downwind, formed by a single wind direction and limited sand; a seif is a long ridge parallel to the wind from two close wind directions; a star dune is a pyramid with several arms where winds blow from many directions.
caption: Figure: barchan, seif and star dunes and the winds that form them (plan view, schematic)

alt: Two-stage formation of a granite dwala: in stage 1 chemical weathering rots closely jointed rock deeply beneath the surface while massive unjointed rock remains as a fresh core; in stage 2 the weathered cover is stripped away, exposing a steep dome (a flank of 180 m in 300 m is a 60 percent gradient, 31 degrees) with a sharp break of slope at its foot.
caption: Figure: two-stage deep weathering and stripping explains a dwala (schematic cross-sections)

alt: Global energy budget of 100 units of sunlight: 26 are reflected by clouds and the air and 4 by the surface (albedo 0.30), 20 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 50 by land and oceans, and the 70 absorbed units must leave as longwave radiation so that inputs equal outputs.
caption: Figure: what happens to 100 units of incoming solar energy (simplified, rounded values)

alt: Height profile across a fault from a digital elevation model: the ground is flat at about 1250 m, drops 76 m over 200 m between 200 and 400 m (gradient 38 percent, angle 20.8 degrees) and is flat again near 1168 m, a throw of 82 m consistent with a normal fault.
caption: Figure: DEM profile across a fault scarp (data from the worked example; height axis starts at 1150 m)

alt: Fault types: under tension a normal fault drops the block above the fault plane (hanging wall), under compression a reverse or thrust fault pushes it up and over, and under shear a strike-slip fault moves the blocks horizontally past each other.
caption: Figure: normal, reverse and strike-slip faults and the stress that makes each

alt: Flood hydrograph: before the catchment was cleared of trees the peak of 38 m3/s stayed below the bankfull discharge of 45 m3/s, but afterwards the peak of 61 m3/s, 60.5 percent higher, exceeds bankfull by 16 m3/s and the river overflows.
caption: Figure: peak discharge before and after clearance against bankfull discharge (peaks and bankfull from the worked example; curve shapes illustrative)

alt: Cross-section of a depression: a cold front undercuts the warm air steeply, lifting it into tall cloud with heavy showers, while at the warm front warm air rises gently over cold air ahead, giving thickening cloud and steady rain.
caption: Figure: a cold front and a warm front in cross-section (schematic)

alt: Gersmehl diagrams: in the tropical rainforest most nutrients (600 of 735 kg per hectare, 82 percent) are in the large biomass circle, with a tiny litter store and rapid wide flows, while in the savanna most (450 of 660 kg per hectare, 68 percent) are in the soil circle and the flows are smaller.
caption: Figure: Gersmehl nutrient diagrams for rainforest and savanna (store sizes from the worked example; flow widths qualitative)

alt: Groynes in plan: they trap sediment moved by longshore drift so the beach builds up on the updrift side and protects the cliff, but little sediment passes them, so the coast further down the drift is starved and erodes faster, as at Mappleton and Cowden on the Holderness coast.
caption: Figure: groynes trap sediment updrift and starve the coast downdrift (plan view, schematic)

alt: Hjulstrom curve (schematic, log scales): medium sand needs the lowest velocity to be eroded, about 20 cm/s; finer silt and clay need higher velocities because particles stick together, and gravel needs more because it is heavy; transport continues at velocities below the erosion curve until the settling curve is crossed and deposition occurs.
caption: Figure: schematic Hjulstrom curve (approximate values) linking flow velocity, particle size and erosion, transport and deposition

alt: Intervisibility profile from station A (1120 m) to station B (1100 m), 6 km apart: the straight line of sight has fallen to 1110 m at 3 km, but the ridge there is 1170 m, 60 m higher, so it blocks the view and B is not visible from A.
caption: Figure: line of sight from A to B and the blocking ridge (values from the worked example; terrain shape schematic)

alt: Limestone karst in cross-section: rain made slightly acid by carbon dioxide from soil and plants dissolves limestone along joints, widening them into shafts, caves and sinkholes, and water drains underground in caves and streams instead of on the surface.
caption: Figure: solution features of a limestone (karst) landscape (schematic cross-section)

alt: Daily rainfall of 14, 31, 96, 188 and 142 mm: the three-day total for days 1 to 3 is 141 mm, below the 300 mm landslide threshold, but days 2 to 4 total 315 mm, so a warning is issued on day 4, and days 3 to 5 reach 426 mm, 126 mm over the threshold.
caption: Figure: three-day rainfall totals against the 300 mm landslide-warning threshold (worked-example data)

alt: Longshore drift in plan: waves arrive at an angle, swash carries sediment up the beach in the direction of the wave, backwash returns it straight down the slope, and the zig-zag path moves the sediment steadily along the coast in one direction.
caption: Figure: longshore drift as a zig-zag path of swash and backwash (plan view)

alt: Lorenz curve for incomes of 400, 500, 700, 900, 1200 and 1800 US dollars in six provinces: the poorest third of provinces receive about 16 percent of income and the poorest half about 30 percent, so the curve bows below the line of equality and the Gini coefficient is 0.28.
caption: Figure: Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient for six provinces (worked-example incomes, illustrative)

alt: Four types of mass movement: heave or creep is a slow movement of damp soil, flow is fast movement of saturated debris like a liquid, a slide moves a block along a surface (curved in a rotational slump), and a fall is rock dropping from a steep jointed cliff.
caption: Figure: heave, flow, slide and fall compared (schematic)

alt: Meander in plan and cross-section: the fastest flow (thalweg) swings to the outer bank of each bend, cutting a steep river cliff, while slow flow on the inside deposits a gently sloping point bar; helicoidal flow carries water to the outer bank at the surface and sediment back along the bed to the inner bank.
caption: Figure: a meander in plan view and in cross-section, showing erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside

alt: Net radiation by latitude: a surplus of +45, +45, +35 and +10 W/m2 in the bands from 0 to 40 degrees, and a deficit growing from -30 W/m2 at 40 to 50 degrees to -115 W/m2 at 80 to 90 degrees; the balance point is at about 37.5 degrees.
caption: Figure: net radiation by latitude band (illustrative values from the lesson table)

alt: Schematic Peltier diagram of mean annual temperature against rainfall: chemical weathering dominates where it is hot and wet (humid tropical, strongest), freeze-thaw dominates where it is cold and moist, thermal and salt weathering matter in hot deserts, and weathering is very slow in dry polar climates.
caption: Figure: schematic Peltier diagram linking climate to the dominant type of weathering (boxes are approximate regions)

alt: Four plate boundary types in cross-section and plan: at a constructive boundary plates move apart and magma forms new crust; at a destructive boundary oceanic crust subducts under continental crust forming a trench and volcanoes; at a collision boundary two continents crumple into fold mountains; at a conservative boundary plates slide past each other with earthquakes.
caption: Figure: the four types of plate boundary (schematic)

alt: Actual and expected town populations under the rank-size rule: the largest city has 1800 thousand people, but towns of rank 2 to 5 have 520, 410, 210 and 190 thousand, well below the 900, 600, 450 and 360 the rule predicts, giving a primacy index of 3.5, so the country has a primate city.
caption: Figure: actual populations compared with the rank-size rule for five towns (worked-example data, illustrative)

alt: The same landscape stored two ways: the vector model keeps exact points, lines and polygons (a borehole, a road and a lake), while the raster model records one value per grid cell so the lake and road edges become stair-steps; halving the cell size gives four times as many cells.
caption: Figure: the same lake, road and borehole as vector features and as a raster grid (schematic)

alt: Scatter graph of maize yield against seasonal rainfall for eight seasons with the least-squares line y = -1.06 + 0.0044x: yield rises with rainfall, the estimate of 1.60 t/ha at 600 mm lies inside the data range (interpolation), but the estimate of 3.37 t/ha at 1000 mm is extrapolation and unreliable.
caption: Figure: regression line for rainfall and maize yield, showing interpolation and extrapolation (worked-example data, illustrative)

alt: Age of ocean-floor basalt rises in a straight line from 0 at the ridge axis to 36 million years at 900 km, a steady spreading rate of 25 km per million years, which is 25 mm a year on each side of the ridge.
caption: Figure: age of basalt against distance from a mid-ocean ridge (illustrative drilling data)

alt: Sediment budget of a beach: inputs of 40 000 m3 from cliff erosion, 15 000 m3 from a river and 10 000 m3 from the sea floor total 65 000 m3 a year, outputs of 50 000 m3 by longshore drift and 5 000 m3 by dredging total 55 000 m3, so the net gain is 10 000 m3 a year and the beach builds out.
caption: Figure: inputs and outputs of a beach sediment budget (worked-example values; arrow thickness shows size)

alt: Travel-time graph for seismic waves: P waves at 6.0 km/s and S waves at 3.5 km/s drift further apart with distance, and a lag of 12 seconds between the first P and S arrival corresponds to a distance of about 101 km from the epicentre.
caption: Figure: P and S wave travel times and the S–P lag method for finding distance to the epicentre (worked-example speeds)

alt: Three models of slope development: in slope decline the whole slope becomes gentler and lower; in parallel retreat the scarp keeps the same angle while it moves back and a pediment widens; in slope replacement a gentle lower slope grows at the expense of the steep upper slope.
caption: Figure: slope decline, parallel retreat and slope replacement compared (schematic profiles at three times)

alt: Surveyed slope profile from the worked example: angles rise from 3 to 24 degrees over the first five sections (convex, waxing slope), stay at 24 degrees over sections 5 to 7 (constant slope) and fall to 4 degrees over sections 8 to 10 (concave, waning slope); total height 24.1 m over 96.0 m, a mean gradient of 25 percent.
caption: Figure: the surveyed slope profile plotted from the angles in the worked example (calculated from 10 sin and 10 cos of each angle; height scale slightly exaggerated)

alt: Soil catena on a granite slope: topsoil depth increases from 20 cm at the crest through 35, 60 and 80 cm to 100 cm in the vlei, while clay rises from 10 to 65 percent and pH from 5.2 to 6.6, because water and fine particles move downslope and collect at the bottom.
caption: Figure: soil depth, clay and pH down a granite catena (worked-example data; slope shape schematic)

alt: Spectral signatures from four bands: healthy maize reflects little blue and red but 0.52 in near infrared (NDVI 0.82), dry bare soil rises steadily from 0.12 to 0.28 (NDVI 0.12), a tarred road is low and flat (0.10 to 0.13), and clear water is dark and falls to 0.02 in near infrared (NDVI minus 0.33).
caption: Figure: reflectance of maize, soil, water and a tarred road in four bands (worked-example values, illustrative)

alt: Spit formation in plan: longshore drift carries sediment along the coast and, where the coast changes direction, deposits it beyond the bend as a ridge in sheltered water; waves from a second direction curve the end into a hook and saltmarsh forms in the sheltered water behind.
caption: Figure: how a spit forms and its parts (plan view, schematic)

alt: Storm hydrograph: rainfall peaks at 18 mm/h in hour 3; the urban stream peaks at 26 m3/s in hour 5 (lag 2 hours) and the rural stream at 10 m3/s in hour 7 (lag 4 hours), so urban surfaces give a shorter lag and a peak 2.6 times higher.
caption: Figure: storm hydrographs for a rural and an urban stream (data from the worked example, illustrative)

alt: Number of streams falls steeply with Strahler order: 36 first-order, 9 second-order, 2 third-order and 1 fourth-order stream, giving bifurcation ratios of 4.0, 4.5 and 2.0 and a mean of 3.5.
caption: Figure: number of streams by order and the bifurcation ratios of the worked-example basin (illustrative data)

alt: Subduction zone cross-section: earthquake foci at depths of 70, 140, 210 and 280 km lie 100, 200, 300 and 400 km from the trench along a plate dipping at 35 degrees beneath the continent, marking the Benioff zone, with a composite volcano above the descending slab.
caption: Figure: earthquake foci along a subducting plate (Benioff zone); depths and distances from the worked example

alt: Secondary succession on an abandoned maize field: plant cover rises from 35 to 95 percent, species from 9 to 28 per 100 square metres, soil organic matter from 1.1 to 3.5 percent and mean height from 0.4 to 9.0 m over 40 years, with organic matter rising more slowly after year 15.
caption: Figure: four measures of an abandoned field over 40 years (worked-example data, illustrative)

alt: Tri-cellular model for one hemisphere: in the Hadley cell air rises at the equatorial low and sinks at about 30 degrees, returning as the trade winds; in the polar cell air sinks at the pole and rises at 60 degrees, flowing out as polar easterlies; the Ferrel cell between them has westerlies at the surface.
caption: Figure: the three cells of the global atmospheric circulation, with pressure belts and surface winds

alt: Cross-section of a tropical cyclone: warm sea supplies heat and moisture, air spirals in at the surface, rises in the towering eyewall clouds with the strongest winds and heaviest rain, flows out at the top, and sinks in the calm clear eye at the centre; outer rain bands surround the storm.
caption: Figure: structure of a tropical cyclone (schematic cross-section)

alt: Water per person against stress thresholds: with 14.25 billion cubic metres a year, 1500 m3 per person for 9.5 million people lies in the stress band (1000 to 1700), and falls to 1140 m3 for 12.5 million people, still stressed but closer to the scarcity limit of 1000 m3.
caption: Figure: water available per person against the stress and scarcity thresholds (worked-example values, illustrative)

alt: Waterfall formation: where resistant hard rock overlies softer rock the soft rock is undercut, the overhanging hard rock collapses, and the fall retreats upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge downstream and a plunge pool at its base.
caption: Figure: how a waterfall forms and retreats upstream, leaving a gorge

alt: Wind transports sediment in three ways: fine silt and clay travel in suspension high in the air, sand grains bounce along the surface in saltation (the main process, up to about a metre high), and coarse grains roll along the ground by traction.
caption: Figure: suspension, saltation and traction in wind transport (schematic)
